utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Matthew Olmsted; case manager, Thomas Laugel; legal intern, Kathryn Fox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps a short oral ruling about the Prosecution motion to modify e-court regarding Exhibits P01378.1351, P01188, P02072, and P02073. Motion was filed on the 10th of July. Prosecution seeks to attach the B/C/S translation of P01378.1351 in e-court, which pertains to an UNPROFOR report. Prosecution also seeks to attach one-page maps to Exhibits P01188, P02072, and P02073, none of which currently contain pages in e-court. Could the Defence give us a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Motion is granted, and the Registrar shall mark the translation and the maps as admitted into evidence. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. Do you understand me -- do you -- sorry, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dusan Jaksic, born on the 2nd of November, 1956, in the village of Rabljak, Nasice municipality, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Can I ask you to make the solemn declaration now that the Court Usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jaksic. You may be seated. Mr. Olmsted, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me begin by asking you, have you previously testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In what case was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In General Mrksic's case seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, who called you as a witness in that case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Defence for Mr. Mrksic, attorney-at-law, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And prior to testifying here today, did you have an opportunity to review that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you have any changes to the evidence you provided in that case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to touch on your background a little bit. First, may I ask you, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you please tell us about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I have high school education.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did you attend high school?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after secondary school, did you attend any other schools?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: When I was serving in the army, I attended the school for reserve officers. At first, I started studying at the traffic school and then when on to the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where was that reserve officer school?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At Bilica. It was the school for the reserve officers of the land forces, infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at some point after your completion of the reserve officers' school, did you return to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was in Vukovar from 1971, so I did my schooling there, and then I went to the army. Once I completed my military service, I went back to Nasice only to de-register myself from the military records in that municipality so that I may be able to return to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand. Can you tell us what year you were back in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I came to Vukovar to attend school there in 1971. I was there throughout my time until the military service, and then after completing the military service, I went back there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And -- and that's what I'm getting at, Mr. Jaksic. After you completed your military service, what year did you return to Vukovar. Could you tell us what year it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you returned to Vukovar, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Previously I worked part-time for Cazmatrans and for a private business. When I went back, I started working for Cazmatrans yet again, and three months later I had a steady job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you hold any position in the Vukovar TO structure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As soon as I served the army, my compulsory service, I was the commander of the scouts platoon of the brigade. That was the assignment I was given immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you referred to a brigade. Was that the TO brigade in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The TO brigade, yes, in the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you hold any subsequent positions in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: After the first exercise with the reconnaissance or scouts platoon, I was commended for my service. I was promoted and sent for training for security officer, and therefore during [as interpreted] the war, I became --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the exact title that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, the interpreters asked us for you to repeat the exact title that you had.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was chief of security of the Vukovar TO brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just noticed one error in transcript. Because the witness said "until the war" not "during the war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we clarify that, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you clarify what Defence counsel has raised.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Territorial Defence and the brigade were operational until the multi-party elections in the area. Subsequently, the ZNG took over the municipality, and the brigade no longer existed. It wasn't being assembled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before we get into all that, I think the clarification is simply how long did you hold the position of head of security for the TO brigade. I -- the question is whether it was until the conflict began or you continued in that position afterwards.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We had exercised up until the multi-party elections. Thereafter, there were no exercises organised anymore, nor did we have any contacts with the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in what part of Vukovar did you live?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I lived on Solidarnost Street, which joins up with Petrova Gora Street at -- once this whole area used to be called Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on e-court 65 ter 6318. This is tab 43. And perhaps we could enlarge it. I think that's probably about right there. Well -- yeah, let's not move it too much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we move it further up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, actually, if we could move it further down so I can show you where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah. And zoom out a little bit as well, please. Let's just leave it there. I think that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's -- yeah, let me ask you a question. First of all, can you -- you just mentioned the area of Sajmiste. Could you take the electronic pen and just circle the area of Sajmiste for us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: You have to move further down so that I could show you the area of Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Is that good right there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you could circle the area of Sajmiste for us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so we can recall your evidence, if you could put an S there for Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I write in Cyrillic script. Is that fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll put at S, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you also mentioned Petrova Gora. Could you tell us, is that a subset of Sajmiste? Is that a smaller component of Sajmiste?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It's a small part of it. As you look at the picture, it's on the left-hand side. It's one of the side streets. It's called Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we sometimes during this trial heard of the area called Petrova Gora. Is that synonymous with Sajmiste, or is it a smaller area? I know it's also a street.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Later on, in the course of war and after the war, since a large defence exercise was organised at -- there, at Petrova Gora previously, the entire area of Sajmiste was then called Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We've also heard the -- a part of Vukovar referred to as Leva Supoderica. Could you circle that for us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for our reference, could you place a letter L inside that circle.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what was the pre-conflict ethnic composition of these neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict, Vukovar was a multi-ethnic town. There were around 38 ethnic groups and minorities living there. We called it Yugoslavia in miniature. The left side of it was prevalently inhabited by the Serbs and the right side of it, the area called Mitnica, et cetera, was predominantly inhabited by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you circle for us Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And again, for our benefit, if you could put a letter M in that circle.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May be this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, prior to the conflict how was the TO organised in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was organised at municipal level. The municipal organs appointed the commander of the staff, and they financed the unit. The next level was the level of the district. That was the level of Slavonia and Baranja, as far as we were concerned and then you had the republic level. So you had a local staff, a district staff, and a republican staff. And, of course, the command structures followed the same principle, when we talk about the commands of brigades and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And organisationally was the TO separate from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned previously that you were part of the Vukovar TO brigade. Was that the only TO you -- overall unit that existed in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was the regular army in Vukovar at the time, as well as the Territorial Defence, and civilian protection. There were also local guards. And these were the structures that were the reserve forces that were to be activated in the event of an aggression or natural disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Within Vukovar municipality, was there any structure that was superior to the Vukovar TO brigade? Was there any unit above it within Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vukovar? Only the political structure, not one in terms of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And to what degree did the ethnic composition of the Vukovar TO brigade reflect the population in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The composition of the brigade reflected the ethnic makeup in the area. The only difference was where the specific battalions or platoons were from. So it would happen that some of these battalions would be predominantly Croat or predominantly Serb, depending on the area that they covered and the population that inhabited the area. That was the situation in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were the TO weapons stored?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was very expensive for municipalities and the country as a whole to build specific-purpose storage facilities, and the army already had its own storage facilities, so the weapons would be stored in their facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were those facilities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was in the forest of Djergaj. It's on the edge of Vukovar in the direction of Brsadin it was by the roadside. It was a storage facility for weapons, explosives and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to those weapons during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think that as the conflict broke out, it was the Brsadin territorials who got there first because they were close by, and they took over the TO weapons. At the time, the army was still under a blockade. There was only one platoon of it deployed that was there for security for the storage facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, this Brsadin TO, was that a -- a TO that formed by the -- the Serb authorities in Brsadin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, territorial units were formed in villages. So it was no longer the case that you had a territorially based structure. It was, rather, individual villages that got organised, and in the area of Petrova Gora, we had roughly 80 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand. In Brsadin, what was the ethnic majority of that village?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be instructed to speak a bit more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, the interpreter has asked that you speak a bit more slower for her. Thank you. Could you tell us, and I think you alluded to this earlier, was the Vukovar TO brigade ever activated in 1990 or 1991 for war operations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, prior to 1991, was there a Petrova Gora TO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in what month was a Petrova Gora TO unit formed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The unit was formed shortly before the liberation of the barracks. However, the organisation was already there. As soon as the multi-party system took hold, we organised village guards, or local guard, to watch over the various settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that the unit was formed shortly before the liberation of the barracks. Can you tell us what month that unit was formed.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was sometime after the 2nd of May, after the events at Borovo Selo, when Vukovar was completely blocked off. It may have been July. The end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By -- by the end of July, could you tell us, how many -- or perhaps you could tell us what percentage of Serbs remained in Vukovar by the end of July?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Women and children and many people in general had already fled Vukovar by that time. Whoever was able to leave no longer went to work or walked about the town. Many Serbs left Vukovar too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did your family leave by that time, by the end of July?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: My family, my wife and four children, left for Kragujevac, and it was it was at the eleventh hour, basically, that they managed to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, initially how many members were -- were there in the Petrova Gora TO unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Initially, we had 180 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did these members come from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They were all residents of these several streets there, and there was some of them who had come over from Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was the commander of this unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, what was the first significant combat operation that members of the Petrova Gora TO participated in?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date. It was before the barracks was liberated that we were attacked once or twice. We received word from the Croats that they -- from the Croat side that they were planning an attack from Mitnica on Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you alluded to the issue. Did your TO unit participate in the liberation of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The liberation of the barracks wasn't along the axis of the barracks. It was along the street before the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I understand. But please focus on my question. Did your TO unit, the Petrova Gora TO, participate in the liberation of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We were issued with the task, we were involved in the action, but along the axis that concerned the barracks, there was the battalion that was called Negoslavci, the Negoslavci battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Could you tell us what date the operation to liberate the barracks occurred on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to that operation, did you make contact with any JNA command in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Perhaps two weeks earlier on, the barracks was under a blockade for over 20 days. We didn't have any electricity, telephone lines or any water. We didn't know what was happening. We had been completely cut off. And then I decided that we should break through to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you reach Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because Atar was on the left-hand side of Petrova Gora and I sent in a platoon. We knew that the troops were by Smetiste, in the direction of Petrovci so that the -- we sent a platoon so that they wouldn't fall into an ambush. We linked up with the troops and they took me to the command of the Mitrovica Brigade in the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who did you meet with in the Mitrovica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Ilija Lokic [as interpreted], who was the command of the Mitrovica Brigade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The transcript says "Lieutenant-Colonel Lokic." Could you confirm whether that's his correct last name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Jokic, J. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did you tell Colonel Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I told Colonel Jokic about our situation, about what we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did he respond?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I then suggested we should liberate the barracks. However, he said that he didn't have such authority and that I would have to contact someone higher up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after this meeting with Colonel Jokic, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I then went to Borovo Selo, near Jakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction to see Ilija Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was Ilija Kojic at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Ilija Kojic replaced Soskocanin, the late Soskocanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what position did he replace the late Soskocanin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Soskocanin was the commander for the defence of the village of Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And had you known Mr. Kojic before this occasion in September?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't known him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Kojic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I can't remember whether I met him on one occasion prior to that event. And, if so, I can't remember where that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting him in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In May, in the 2nd of May, I was in my village when the attack was launched on Borovo Selo. I only managed to get to Vukovar. We went to Trpinje by car and then carried on to Vukovar on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand you didn't meet him on the 2nd of May. But any time in May, did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Regardless, you knew who he was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew he worked in the police and that he held that post at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, why did you meet with Mr. Kojic in Borovo Selo after your meeting with Colonel Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, because Borovo Selo was more organised. I thought that he now had more authority and that it would be easier for me to get to the corps command through him. They were -- probably recognise his authority sooner than mine. So given his authority, once I had presented the situation to them, I thought it would be easier for us to exert an influence in the sense of acting so that the barracks could be liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after you met with Mr. Kojic, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We went to Novi Sad, to the command of the Novi Sad Corps, to see General Bratic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did Mr. Kojic accompany you on that trip?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did you and Mr. Kojic tell General Bratic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I told General Bratic about the entire situation, since, in Vukovar, there were 50 or 60 volunteers. My brother, brother-in-law, were in the barracks in Vukovar, so I knew quite a lot about the situation through phone calls. I had heard that there had been quite a few wounded. They had no water, no food. Snipers fired on them constantly and they came under mortar fire, constant mortar fire, and it wasn't possible for the barracks to survive if no one reacted. So I suggested we should attempt to liberate the barracks and to liberate the troops who were confined within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did General Bratic respond?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Bratic only said, Very well, either contact Jokic and agree everything with him concerning further action to be contain in order to liberate the barracks. You will then have your agreement with him as to how you should proceed. I then contacted Jokic, and we then agreed on what action should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was agreed between you and Colonel Jokic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I received uniforms from Jokic for those who had no uniforms. I received weapons, automatic weapons, so I had a group of 42 men that I equipped, and we tried to link up with the troops and clear the Proleterska Street. And I was also provided with a RUP-12 radio device.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there to be a signal for the beginning of the operation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't tell me exactly when the attack would be launched. He said I should wait. There would be a signal, and that would be when birds flew over the Vukovar shelter. That would be the sign for us to go into action --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, when there were fighter planes flying over the area, that would be the signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the fighter planes, did they, in fact, fly over the area on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They did. That was the sign for me to turn the radio device on, and they then launched rockets against the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What did the rockets hit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They targeted the warehouse. As to what they hit, I didn't go there to observe it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the name of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was only two rockets, and they weren't very potent. These Galeb planes are fairly small planes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I see that the transcript omitted that it was Vukovar Zenga shelter. It was in line 11, page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment. So the name of the shelter would be ZNG; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: ZNG used it as their shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. ZNG used it. That's what you mean, yes. ZNG used it as their shelter. Is that right, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I just would ask in the future if such situations that Defence counsel simply say that there needs to be a clarification regarding a particular part of the transcript rather than providing what he believes was said, just to make sure that we're getting the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If need be, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say that it is recorded and it will be -- see from the -- from the audio record what the witness originally said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's right. Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This warehouse, what was the name of the warehouse? Did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was in a basement where equipment was kept. It was dug in. It had strong walls and it was quite secure. It was in the basement of the Vuteks company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. That was what I was after. Thank you. Now, what units participated in the operation that day, on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Mitrovica Brigade was involved, Petrova Gora company and the Negoslavci battalion on the axis up to the barracks. As for those involved on the other side, in other areas, I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You referred to a Negoslavci battalion. Was that JNA or was that a TO battalion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did any of these units reach the barracks that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Negoslavci unit did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 6318 on the screen. This is, again, tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, if you could take the pen again and mark for us, after this operation occurred, what area of Vukovar was under the control of the JNA and its -- the TO units that participated in that operation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: What units participated -- after the second day --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me -- let me clarify the question. After the operation was completed, what area --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: On the first day, we were blocked by a wagon in Proleterska Street so we didn't reach Vuteks on -- on the first day. It was only on the second day that we reached that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand, and unfortunately I do not have time to go into all the details of the operation. What I want you to answer is after this operation was completed on the first or second day, can you tell us, can you draw a line as to what area was --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, a line. Where the -- where the front line was essentially after that operation. And do we need to scroll down a bit for you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be like this. That was the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you put a B on the barracks.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. So everything below that line was under control of the JNA and the other TO units.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: And the TO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, at some point, did the JNA Guards Motorised Brigade arrive in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade arrived on the 2nd of October. That's when they arrived in Vukovar -- or, rather, on the 1st, but on the 2nd, the Guards Brigade went into action. It was brought in on the 1st at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the arrival of the Guards Brigade, did anything happened organisationally to the Petrova Gora TO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Petrova Gora TO, since this area was liberated, and there were Serb inhabitants there, they immediately mobilised in the Petrova Gora brigade. There were some volunteers. I formed a company. I had about 344 men for combat, plus logistics. There were about 20 men in logistics and then there were men to provide security for Vuteks and Trend [phoen], for these companies that had been liberated. These men were slightly elderly. They were there to provide security for the factories so that they could prevent looting. So, at the time, there were about 344 men on the line ready for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, at this stage, was the Petrova Gora TO unit, was it a brigade, a battalion? What was it -- what kind of unit was it at that stage?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At the time it was a battalion. Since it was independent, not on the TO, as part of brigade, so we called it a detachment because it acted independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you explain to us, what that means, that the detachment acted independently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: A battalion is part of a brigade. But a detachment is the size of a battalion but acts independently so it's not part of the brigade. It's independent. It doesn't have a superior commander, but the commander of this so-called battalion is independent. They can act independently. They can penetrate the rear and get involved in actions independently without being linked to the brigade command. So it wasn't part of that composition. It was independent. It represented a sort of independent formation and was not integrated within a larger body.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many companies were in the TO detachment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Four companies at the time, but the composition was not identical for each one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who were the commanders of those four companies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The company commanders: Miroljub Vujovic was the company commander for the 1st Company; the 2nd Company, Stanko Vujanovic; the commander of the 3rd one was Miroslav Pejic; and the commander of the 4th Company was Sinisa Fot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did any of these commanders have training as officers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any reserve officers there at the time. Only my deputy was a reserve officer, and those who were the most competent, the most courageous, well, they would designate commanders. First they'd be commanders of platoons and they would subsequently become company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, how big was Miroljub Vujovic's company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, last time I had a notebook so I was able to use that. But I think there were about 117 men in his company. His company was the biggest one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how about Mr. --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: And their main axis was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how about Mr. Vujanovic's company? How big was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the number exactly now because on the previous occasion in Mrksic I had a notebook and then I was able to provide all the information by relying on the notebook. Perhaps about 200 and -- perhaps about 70, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was an operational group formed in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar there was the Southern Operations Group. While we were co-ordinating action with the Mitrovica Brigade, there was the commander, Colonel Bajo Bojat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was Colonel Bojat replaced; and, if so, when, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bajo Bojat was replaced perhaps a week or two later by General Mrksic. He was Colonel Mrksic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you attend briefings with Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How frequently would you attend briefings with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were those briefings held?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At his command post in Negoslavci village. That was the command of the south operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was Major Sljivancanin during the operations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was the chief of security of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, did -- did Major Sljivancanin limit himself to security matters or did he expand his mandate during the operations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of service valid before the war, at a time of war, the commander had authority and the chief of security. That was also the case on this occasion. Colonel Mrksic said that the command and the security organ should exercise authority in the operations group -- Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who was more often in Vukovar, Mrksic or Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was there almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was Major Sljivancanin's relationship with the media?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, he always had the media and cameras in tow. Wherever he went, they would accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As TO commander, did you meet with members of the district government, the SBWS district government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I never did so officially. Only when I went to Erdut I unofficially passed through. I unofficially contacted them just to say hello, but I didn't have any official meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who from the SBWS government would you have contact with?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I had contact with Rade Leskovac. I'd seen Dokmanovic there, too. I was on good terms with him before the war. I remember Goran giving me an emblem, a Serbian flag, an emblem that I could put on my cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You just referred to "Goran." Could you tell us the last name of that person?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you came to Erdut, did you meet with anyone in the armed forces structure in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I went to see the commander of Operational Group North, Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, when I was in Erdut. Since the training centre and the palace are near to each other, as I was waiting for a good moment to cross over to Serbia, I only dropped by to see them for a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The transcript reads that you went to see the commander of Operational Group North, Mr. Radovan Stojicic. Can you clarify what his position is or what you believed his position to be at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: TO. I don't know if it was -- I know that he was the commander of the TO Operational Group --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be asked to repeat this. It was very unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, but if you could repeat your last answer for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Badza was the commander of the TO of the operational -- Operations Group North.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of your meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I went twice, and both times, it was to co-ordinate with the operations group, to co-ordinate our activity. And the second time was to see that co-ordinated action was put in place with Mrksic. So I went there personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware of a unit called the Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what kind of unit was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think that they belonged to the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you remember who the commander of that unit was:

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni. I don't remember the others at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that unit was subordinated to any JNA command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: All the units in the area were subordinated to the command of the Operational Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you see any of the leaders of the Radical Party in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Seselj when he was touring the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when and where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He passed down Petrova Gora Street and Solidarnost Street. He went through to the front line to boost the morale and to visit the troops in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what month that occurred?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. It was probably in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there other volunteer units from Serbia --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Early November. There were quite a few volunteers who were members of military units and territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how were these volunteers viewed by the OG South Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't perceive a difference in the treatment of soldiers or TO members. I didn't see that there was a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'm speaking about volunteers from Serbia. What was the attitude or what was the perception of the JNA command towards them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that we didn't have any problems whatsoever with volunteers from Serbia. They were patriots, honest folk, for the most part, and if they were in the army, they were assigned to a platoon or a company, and if they were TO, they were subordinated to us, and they were not extremist at all. They didn't cause any trouble, quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware whether any members of these volunteer units or members of volunteer engaged in any crimes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any organised volunteer units other than that organised by the Radical Party. The rest were all members of the TO. At any rate, they didn't have their own independent units. They were either members of the TO or the JNA or members of the unit belonging to the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were you aware whether any of these volunteer, regardless of what unit or -- they were attached to, were you aware whether they were committing any crimes in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that during combat, it could not so happen that they would loot and plunder and carry on any of the looted goods across the check-points, because that was very strict. It could only have happened after the liberation of Vukovar. That was when the -- the control was not as strict as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the issue of volunteer crimes ever come up at any of your briefings with Colonel Mrksic or Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: When I attended briefings, there were no such comments made, as far as I remember, up until the 17th of November. There were no such cases being reported in the operative sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was a TO Staff established in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, a TO Staff was set up in Vukovar. A TO Staff was set up in Oriolik for OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: That was sometime in October, I think, when the Guards Brigade was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to October, was there an effort to establish a TO Staff for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Two weeks before the 14th of September, Jokic and I had preparations for the liberation of the barracks. Slobodan Grahovac and Mile Uzelac dropped by, came to the hotel, intent on setting up a TO Staff of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who were these individuals at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Mile Uzelac was the pre-war commander of the Vukovar TO Staff, and I saw Slobodan Grahovac for the first time on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the time, though, in September 1991, what organ were they with?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I found out later that Slobodan Grahovac had been working for the MUP of the then -Yugoslavia. I only know that he was in the Ministry of Interior of Yugoslavia. What specifically he did, I didn't know. I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way: Where did Mr. Uzelac and Mr. Grahovac come from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It must have been from Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was in Sid that they came from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I know that there was a mobilisation staff in Sid. There, they mobilised the individuals in the area and deployed them to where we were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Grahovac was from, as far as where he lived prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I found out that he was Vukovar-born, but I never met him in Vukovar. It was later through stories that I came to recall his mother and where she worked. I never saw him though. He was probably sent to study in Belgrade, and I never saw him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what profession did Mr. Uzelac have prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In 1971, when I started high school, Mr. Uzelac was my maths teacher for that one year. At that point, he was appointed commander of the Vukovar TO Staff. He taught my generation through to the end of schooling, although he was already working for the staff. But, as I say, in 1971, he transferred as a commander of Vukovar TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Grahovac and Mr. Uzelac came to Vukovar, did you speak with them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As they came, I was just about to see Commander Jokic. They joined me, and they said that they wanted to see how this should be put in place. And I said, Look, where have you been so far? It's just now that it's occurred to you that you should set up this staff. Now that it's all done and you've come to -- to -- with this idea. I'm not interested. And that's where it all ended. So I left them there, and I went to see Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that a TO Staff was eventually established in Vukovar in October 1991. Who was appointed TO Staff commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know. I was at the front line when I learned that there was a meeting held in Oriolik where I was appointed TO commander and Mile Uzelac, my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did this TO Staff of which you became commander did it encompass only Vukovar town or did it encompass a wider area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The entire OG South. It was the staff of OG South, TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us roughly -- I'm sure you don't know the exact number, but roughly how many village TO Staffs were subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were more than 20 villages, and all the units that were there, including Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where was the TO Staff in Vukovar headquartered?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was only Velepromet that had offices, and it was not destroyed. We decided to set up our staff in those offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now did you fully assume the duties of TO Staff commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was appointed TO Staff commander, but I could not discharge solely that duty. Mrksic did not allow for that because then the Petrova Gora unit would be without a leader. He said that it was important for us to liberate Vukovar and that the commander of TO Staff was a political function and that we should now focus on the liberation of Vukovar. Consequently, I had to stay with the Petrova Gora unit until the liberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In what way is TO Staff commander a political function?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was a political function because, let's say, the TO finances, equips and appoints municipal TO commanders. So it's not a military structure; it's a municipal/civilian structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do TO Staffs fall under a government institution; and, if so, which institution?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They all fall under the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You -- you mentioned that you had this conversation with Mrksic regarding his desire for you to focus on -- on the efforts to liberate Vukovar. Who performed the duties of TO Staff commander in your absence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Whenever there was no combat or operations in course, I would attend meetings. So whenever there was a truce in place, I was able to attend meetings. Otherwise, when fighting was going on, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you just said. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: If I went for a meeting, then I would -- my deputy, Milanovic [as interpreted], Milan would take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The transcript says your deputy "Milanovic." Could you actually confirm whether he was your deputy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Ivanovic. Milan Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about Mile Uzelac? Did he perform any roles when you weren't available as TO Staff commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Mile was my deputy. When I could not attend meetings, he did, in my stead. But I think that there were two meetings that both of us attended. I recall myself, him, and Lazo Pjevic going to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you're changing topics? I mean about the witness's deputy. There is a little bit of confusion there about Milan Ivanovic. You asked whether he was your deputy, and then the witness says that Mile is his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We should clarify that, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what position did Milan Ivanovic hold within the TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Milan Ivanovic was deputy commander of the Petrova Gora detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, Mile Uzelac was deputy of the TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Uzelac was deputy commander of the TO Staff of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so we have everyone on the record, were there also assistant commanders of the TO Staff; and, if so, could you name them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was Lazo Pjevic, he was for mobilisation. Jovica Kresovic was for communications. Pajo Stekovic was operator. This was 22 years ago ... it's a bit hard. Mile was deputy; Mile Uzelac. There was one man from Trpinje. He was in charge of engineers. He was also a reserve officer. I can't recall his name. I had everything noted down in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Not a problem. We understand a long time --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Many of them had not attended military exercises with me previously. They had not been members of the TO brigade. So I only got to know them at this point; whereas, all the others who had been there with me previously, senior officers, I knew them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Jaksic. I think we have two minutes, so let me quickly show you document P1727. This is tab 4. And we see this document is issued by Dusan Filipovic. Who was he back in --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe this -- who was he back in October 1991, the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Dusan Filipovic, I only knew that Slobodan Grahovac was staff commander. Dusan Filipovic was a member of the staff, but I didn't know which organ he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see a couple stamps on this document. Have you seen those stamps before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It says "chief."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive a single document with such a stamp. It's the first time I'm seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Jaksic, this is the time for our first break. We take 30 minutes and come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have to apologise for the -- for the delay. It's entirely my mistake. I was working in my office and completely forgot about the time. Sorry about that. Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, before the break, you mentioned TO Staff meetings. Can you tell us, did any representatives of the village TO Staffs attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who from the villages attended those meetings, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At the time of the war, they were commander of units in the village. Those were both commanders of units and presidents of the villages. And they were the people who attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned one of the meetings was in -- was in Lovas. Do you recall who were the representatives from Lovas?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think Devetak, Ljuban Devetak, was the president of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And generally what was discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The general subject concerned war-time activities, the conditions for mobilisation, organising matters in the field. Since the civilian authorities were not properly functioning, one was concerned about the families of men on the battle-field. They had to be taken care of, had to be fuel provided, agricultural matters had to be taken care of, and so on and so forth. So these were basic matters that concerned the inhabitants and the villages. These are the basic issues that were addressed at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did any representatives of the JNA attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that having occurred when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, for how long were you commander of the Petrova Gora detachment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: From the time it was established until more or less the end of the war, the 16th or the 17th - something like that - it was just prior to the operation launched against Leva Supoderica, or, in fact, I apologise, against Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so we're clear on the record, the 16th or 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: According to my notebook, I had a meeting on the 17th. I couldn't even remember it. It was in my notebook. At the time I wasn't the commander of the Petrova Gora detachment, so I attended the meeting as a staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And all I was seeking to clarify, you remained commander of the Petrova Gora detachment until sometime in November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: November. Up to the time just prior to the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Sljivancanin appointed Milivoj Vojovic [as interpreted] to replace me as the commander of the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin provide with you any reasons why he was replacing you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. He just said Miroljub, as of today you will be the commander of the Petrova Gora detachment and of the Vukovar TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think you just clarified the question I -- I had. You -- with regard to your question -- earlier answer, it's says on the record he -- that Vojovic was -- replaced you as commander of the 1st Company. But he replaced you as commander of the Petrova Gora TO; is that correct? Is that correct? You were replaced as TO commander of the Petrova Gora detachment.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I've also been reminded to try to correct with regard to the person who replaced you. Can you give us his name one more time? I don't think it's clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin give you any reasons for why he was replacing you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why do you believe you were replaced?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I noticed that Mr. Sljivancanin, and Radic and the others, that they were treating me a little more coldly. Something was going on but I didn't know what. It was only on --at the other trial that I noticed that Mr. Sljivancanin was conducting an operative defence against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Operative -- was processing me operationally, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the time were you -- well, what was he processing you for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: His Defence said that it concerned black marketeering with cars and so on. Apparently I had obtained some property illicitly. I heard that they said I had about 300.000 marks in a bank -- in the Sabac bank, and I was shocked to hear this as I had nothing to do with these matters. I then asked the chief of the police, Djukic, what's going on? Is it possible for them to spread such lies? He said, Why are you concerned? What are they saying about you? Given the lies they are telling, a lot of replacements should have been made years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you just clarify for us, when did you first learn of these allegations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear this from Mr. Sarsic [phoen] but from other people. They conveyed the rumours to me. It all started when four humanitarian aid trailers arrived Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And please just focus on my question. My question was: When did you first hear of these allegations? Just so we have a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it was before the liberation of Vukovar. I'd already been significantly affected by these rumours at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, at the time, were you trying to prevent any kind of activities that might have justified or might -- might have been the reason for your removal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I thought that these were just rumours, that it had nothing to do with the top of the command. It wasn't logical for me, for Mr. Sljivancanin not to have my biography. I couldn't believe that he hadn't checked everything, that he hadn't spoken to me about these matters. I didn't believe he could act in such a way, be involved in such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question to you was: At the time of your removal, or before your removal, were you interfering in any activities that were going on in the Vukovar area that, in retrospect, you believe may have been the reason for your removal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when these six trailers arrived in Vukovar, when I raised the issue, someone just signed this fictitiously and they returned to Vukovar. These -- to Serbia. The goods were sold at the market later. Later I found out that there was a Siptar called Dusan Spasojevic there, who was eliminated in the Sablja Operation, was at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So am I to understand you that you were attempting to prevent smuggling operations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't prevent these activities because the trailers had already left. I only raised the issue and asked for the matter to be looked into. I wanted them to see where the trailers had gone, why the aid hadn't been delivered to the people in Vukovar ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what effect do you believe your removal had on the situation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, as an officer, given my background, my education, I never even thought of doing something illegal, of embezzling anything. This wasn't allowed, in any case. And I was an optical [as interpreted] for certain elements who wanted to get involved in looting and illegal activities, and that was why there was the -- this slandering that concerned myself, and they attributed actions to me that were, in fact, their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that were no longer head of the TO Staff as well. Why did you relinquish that position, of TO Staff commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Since Sljivancanin said at a meeting in the command that he [Realtime transcript read in error "Ilija"] would be head of the TO Staff, I was to be in charge of the OG South and that the Vukovar TO Staff should be subordinated to the OG South Staff. However, he took over complete authority. He was then the commander. And since after the event concerning the trailers, I heard from the military intelligence and from officers in the barracks that preparations were under way to have me eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You -- you mentioned the name Ilija. Could you give us the last name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: When? Just a minute ago or earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript reads: "Since Sljivancanin said at the meeting in," and it's not clear, "the command that Ilija would be head of the TO Staff."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Miroljub. Not Ilija. Miroljub. Miroljub Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you ever see a written order to this effect removing you and appointing Vujovic to this position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I never received a written order, nor did anyone deliver such an order to me. But a few days later, Miroljub waved this in front of me, Petrova Gora, and since I knew what was under way, and I didn't try to do anything against it, he his hand on his pistol. He was waiting for a my reaction. I quite simply decided to relinquish authority. It was either that or lose my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you believe that Vujovic had the qualities to be a TO commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Vujovic didn't have such qualities. He didn't have the mind. He was just a puppet in the hands of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after your removal as TO commander, did you remain within the TO structure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, after the fall of Vukovar, did you get a sense of the sentiment of the Serb population of Vukovar towards the Croats who had participated in the armed conflict there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, in Petrova Gora, in my case, there were neighbours who had stayed on there, who were friends. They remained with us throughout that period, and nothing happened to them. They were protected, as well as other ethnic minorities. On one occasion, they took a hunting rifle from a Rusin [as interpreted] and the rifle was returned to the person immediately after I had intervened. Later when I left, as to what happened, who knows? On one occasion, Milosevic even said that someone should be immediately eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Witness, please -- please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I may interject there. Were members of the Serb population angry at the -- at the Croats who had participated in the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, when blood is spilt after all that evil, all those who lived through that, who experienced that, they held these things against them. They were angry with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to show you a couple of video-clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The first one is 65 ter 4799.14. And we will play the clip until 1 hour, 20 minutes, and 48 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... it should go, a bus or a truck, something will have to ... "We do apologise. This is the footage made by the Politika television crew filmed over the past couple of days in Vukovar. In the following seven to eight minutes, you will hear the testimonies of people as seen through the eye of the camera in the hands of ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We've paused at an image, Mr. Jaksic. Could you tell us, who is the person on the left wearing the uniform?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us when and where this footage was taken.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was on 18th of January [as interpreted]. The civilians went to the bridge on Vutcija [phoen]. I was present there. And the women here were Croats. I found out about that later. I didn't even know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we clarify the record. It says in your last answer it was on the 18th of January. Is January the correct month?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, no. The 18th of November. That was the liberation of Vukovar. Borovo Naselje was on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And at this stage, were you a civilian, or were you still with the TO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At the time everyone had uniforms. I wasn't the commander of the TO then. Jovica Kresovic and I left the staff unofficially to find the wife and relative of a pilot and the son of Kerisic [phoen]. We tried to help the civilians pass through with the help of the brigade. They had subordinated their logistics, the lorries and everything -- or rather, used their logistics and lorries and so on to get the civilians out of Vukovar, as far as Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's jump to 1 hour, 24 minutes and 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Before that, the witness mentioned Kragujevac Brigade but it is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I heard the mention of that brigade. I don't think it needs to be clarified at this stage. If they're going to revise the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you sure about that, Mr. Olmsted? If we can be sure about that, then the problem is solved. But are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I won't say 100 per cent sure. I thought I heard it. I'll ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned a brigade. Can you tell us the name of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was the Zaslin [phoen] detachment from Kragujevac. In the case of action, they had to protect the Zastava factory for special purposes and their cars. They were sent to the Vukovar battle-field where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could now jump to 1 hour, 24 minutes, 33 seconds. In the English transcript, this is in -- on page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to say that they didn't enter the town. They remained in the rear. So the detachment didn't enter the town. That is why I used them so that they could help get the civilians out by placing these lorries and other equipment at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Well, if we could please now go to where -- where I want to start playing again, which is 1 hour, 24 minutes and 33 seconds. This is on page 4 of the English transcript, about halfway down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We'll restart where we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: He couldn't find the passage and the sound quality was too poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. If we can turn to page 4 of the English transcript. I think it's around line 17 that it begins. And I understand it's a little bit difficult to hear. But let's try -- try it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter still cannot find the passage. It sounds as if the person was saying: Everything has been mined. We cannot find the mines. We don't know where the mines are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, I have a different transcript but now we've got it corrected. If we could have the interpreters go to page 6 of the transcript, and we believe this is starting around line 23 of the transcript on page 6. And if we could play it one last time to see if we can get it right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Only, they must have mined it ... just -- no, no. Tomislav is now ... check this ... the biggest criminal. I don't know whether he has been in ... he did not come yesterday ... but now we heard that yesterday ... Tomislav, the biggest criminal ... Dosen ... Molnar ... Dane ... Korac Ivan who swore at me because I am a Serbian woman ... Pedja, name the people. Go on, who else? Pedja, go on, name more of the men that you know ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you assist us? What's -- what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know this lady. I see that she is mentioning certain names and saying that they are terrible criminals. They say that someone insulted her because she was a Serb woman, and this was said to members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the persons she's naming, what ethnicity are they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this clip be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2368.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to show you 65 ter 4797.1. We will play until 1 hour, 6 minutes and 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] On this gloomy day Vukovar has its brighter face. On my left side is a large settlement of the Second Congress. On the right, the famous settlement called Petrova Gora predominantly inhabited by the Serbs. Here it looks like there was no war. Houses were quite -- left quite intact. Life is slowly returning. Good morning is it some family's patron saint's day? "Yes, it is Slava today. "What day is it today for the army? "I don't know. "Is it Arandjelovdan today. "Yes. "You've baked a cake for the army? "Yes, we've baked it for the army. Where are they? "Well, here in this house, everywhere around us they guard us."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, could you identify for us where this footage is taking place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This was filmed in a settlement called Drugi Kongres, the Second Congress. It was the second area to be liberated after the barracks. There was no heavy fighting there and so the settlement wasn't much damaged. She baked this cake for Arandjelovdan. It was meant for a captain who was celebrating his family's patron saint's day. That's what it was for. And she said, The army was there to guard us. And this was -- we are still on the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was one of my questions. So this holiday, what's the date of this holiday, Arandjelovdan Day? What's the date?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
