utterances.text: Yes. Well, it turns out that Arandjelov liberated because Vukovar was liberated on the 17th, Borovo Selo on the 20th, so the 21st was for the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned Second Congress. Where is this in relation to the Sajmiste-Petrova Gora area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It's right next to Sajmiste, or where Sajmiste or the market-place used to be. It's right on the beginning of the Petrovac road, where the Petrovac road starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could jump to 1 hour, 6 minutes and 43 seconds. I understand that the transcript on page 2, has slightly different time code but that is essentially where we're going to begin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] It doesn't look too -- you're not getting too ill here? "No. "So nothing happened to you? "Nothing happened. We are preparing a stew for our captain. It is his family patron saint's day today. "All right. What are your views on all these events in the last four -- three or four or five months? "Everything was horrible. The worst thing is that the neighbours were the first ones doing it. "Sorry for asking, are you Serb? "Yes, yes, I am. And my husband is a Serb and all of us here. "What were the things that your neighbours did to do? "All kinds of things. They were threatening us, maltreating us, turning their heads from us, all sorts of things, shooting at our houses, everything. They're gone now. "Will they come back? "I don't think so but I'd like to see them now. I have heard that they are there at Velepromet. I would like to see them now, look them in their eye and let them see we remained humans while they are more than animals. "Today in Vukovar, in the Oris family this is what things look like. Homely-set table, nicely arranged dining-room."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the anger in the -- in the -- in the Serb population. Is this indicative of that, what she expressed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I know this woman. She does live in this neighbourhood of the Second Congress. So she was liberated on the 14th of September. Her house was free but she was telling us what had been going on before the 14th, that she was being harassed and her house came under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, I do want to try to complete your examination in my time allotted, so it's very important if you could please --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: And she was saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's very important for you to focus on my questions at this stage so we can get through this so that cross-examination can begin. And my question was simply: What she was expressing here, her anger, was that indicative of the feelings among the Serb population at the time. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2369, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, were you at Velepromet in Vukovar on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At what time did you first arrive there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was only thanks to the footage that I realised that I was there on the 20th, sometime in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you were at Velepromet, who arrived?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was at Velepromet, and I recall that there was Mr. Goran Hadzic, Arkan was there, as was Slavko Dokmanovic, president of the municipality, Jagodina, Vlado Kosic and many others. I saw them in the footage. I can't recall them. There were many other people from Vukovar. Milos Vojnovic was there, of course, and I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, in what capacity was Arkan present there that morning?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I saw that Arkan was with Mr. Goran. Was he a accompanying him as an escort, I don't know, because he was head of security at the Erdut training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, just so the record is clear, and I know I keep on asking you this, you've referred now a couple of times to "Goran." Is that in each of those cases Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is again omitted from the transcript that security at the Erdut training centre, the witness said to Badza. It is line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you're referring to, Mr. Zivanovic. Is this a place or a name, a person's name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The name, or nickname, Badza. He was Radovan Stojicic nicknamed Badza --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] TO commander of OG North.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the -- the TO commander, OG North, is that Radovan Stojicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of Operation Group North, yes. Arkan was head of security there for that centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the name of Savo Stupar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight only.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his role was, but I would see him in the company of Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Mr. Stupar was present on the 20th of November at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I saw him in the footage. He was at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But do you personally recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. It was 22 years ago. I saw him in the footage. I recognised him. But my memory doesn't serve me as to whether he was somewhere in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we're still talking about when these government representatives first arrived at Velepromet. Did you learn the reason why they were coming to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I learnt that from Mr. Milos Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you learned from him, as far as why these officials were all coming to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I learned from him that there would be a government meeting and that I should go to see Mrksic, because I was the only one who knew him personally, and plead with him that all the civilians who had blood on their hands, who had committed war crimes and were known to have done so should not be allowed to go to Serbia but should remained within that military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when Mr. -- first of all, can you tell us who Milos Vojnovic was, what position he held?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think that Milos Vojnovic was the president of the district court or minister of justice. But I know that he was the person in charge of the judiciary in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before I ask you some questions about this conversation you had with Mr. Vojnovic, could you tell us, what was the mood amongst you and the other officials who were present at Velepromet that morning?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The mood was euphoric. We congratulated each other on the liberation. It was a festive mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you've now mentioned your conversation with Mr. Vojnovic. Was anyone else present in immediate surroundings when you were having this conversation with Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that Mr. Vojnovic and I were there. We knew each other from before the war. Our children were close friends. I know that we had this inform conversation where he asked me that I should go and see Mrksic and see to it that all those who were war criminals should stay behind, should be tried before the district court because we had competent judges who were able to do that part of the job well and that they should not be allowed to go to Serbia. That was the only issue that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else about what he thought the status of the SBWS government was at the time, as far as its capacity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did he mention anything about the police force?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, I found an entry in my notebook for the 17th of November that negotiations were already under way for Croats to surrender. And there were bullet-points as to what should be done next: That police stations should be set up, that health centres should be set up, that all the various services for civilians should be set up so that there would be normal services provided as well as the cleaning services for the town. There were no supplies, all the shops were destroyed, and life had to be restored to that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you share Mr. Vojnovic's views?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. At first, I did. At that time Serbia was not official in a war. The JNA was, but not Serbia as a republic. That's why we thought that we should not draw Serbia into this. Rather, that the district itself should do its job. The district was already formally as a state, as the RSK, and we wanted to have these people tried in our district rather than in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vojnovic provide you with any details regarding what would be done with these alleged war criminals, if Mr. Mrksic agreed to your request?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. He only said that they should be brought to justice here in the districts, that the courts in the district should be responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to pause before answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, the interpreters have again asked you to -- to slow down a bit and to pause before you answer my question, just so that they're able to interpret everything you say. Was any mention made with regard to where these war criminals were to be detained?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was any mention made as to who would be responsible or what organs would be responsible for the detention of these war criminals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This wasn't discussed at all. The issue discussed was that I should go to see Mrksic to make sure that they would not be sent onto Serbia but that they should be kept there. I suppose that they organised it independently later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, did you, in fact, meet with Colonel Mrksic as requested by Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How soon after your conversation with Vojnovic did you meet with Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: After the conversation we had I went to Negoslavci and didn't stay long with Mr. Mrksic, perhaps some ten to 15 minutes. I went -- I then went back and conveyed Mrksic's views on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did you tell Colonel Mrksic during this -- this brief meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I suggested -- or, rather, I told him what Mr. Vojnovic had said; i.e., that those who were known to have committed crimes should stay in the -- within the district and be tried before the district court. However, he was categorical in saying that they should be sent to Serbia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And can the witness please repeat what he said last.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Jaksic, I know that you just naturally speak very quickly but you're going to have to slow down somewhat for the interpreters. They've asked that you could repeat the very end of what you said.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could just repeat what you said at the very end of your last answer.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He said that the deal was that they could not stay behind, that they should go to Serbia, that he could not allow for them to end up in the hands of the territorials. That's what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on whose behalf did you tell Colonel Mrksic you had come to see him about this issue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Vojnovic, only him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic know who Mr. Vojnovic was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I told him who Vojnovic was. And if he didn't know it before, he knew at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was Colonel Mrksic aware at this time that you no longer were TO commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After this conversation with Colonel Mrksic, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I went back to Velepromet. I conveyed the information to Mr. Vojnovic, stayed there for a short while and headed back to Petrova Gora. I passed by the barracks on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we'll get to that in a moment. Can you tell us, approximately -- I know a long time has passed, approximately how long -- how much time elapsed between when you were first at Velepromet, when the government officials first arrived, and when you returned from your meeting with Colonel Mrksic? Can you tell us how long a period are we talking about? Was it a half an hour? An hour?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately 45 minutes, an hour -- half an hour to 45 minutes. That would include going there and back and the meeting I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, while you were back at Velepromet and you informed Mr. Vojnovic of your conversation with Colonel Mrksic, did you do anything else at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. That was the only thing. I do remember that tensions were high for the army. They were terribly angry at the army, and tensions were high in that respect. I don't recall anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that "they were terribly angry at the army." Who's "they"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, almost the entire room. It wasn't just one individual that I would recall standing up. Everyone was. The whole room was practically murmuring and speaking out against the army, saying that they were protecting the Ustasha and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned a room. What was this room?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The room at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you recall who do you remember was in the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact names, really. I remembered what I saw in the footage. It was 22 years ago. Besides, I tried to put behind and forget all these events that happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These people are in -- in a room at Velepromet. Who are these people and what is going on in this room? What event is going on in this room?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: You mean at the government meeting or the people at Velepromet, the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You referred to a government meeting. You've described that tensions were high. Was this at the government meeting, that tensions were high?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That was -- that was more than the government members. Who was there? I really don't know. Was it the territorials? The workers there? There were far more than there were cabinet members.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What -- which cabinet members were at this meeting, Mr. Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I know that cabinet members at the time included Mr. Goran Hadzic. I saw Dokmanovic. I saw Crnogorac, Mica, for transport. I remember Rade Leskovac. Boro Bogunovic was there for transport. But I don't recall seeing him there. Devetak was in charge of commerce, as far as I remember. I'm not sure, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, just roughly, how long were you at this -- this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was there for a very short time. I said what I had to say to Mr. Vojnovic, and before that, Mr. Goran Hadzic expressed his wish for me to take him to Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Besides members of the government present at this meeting, do you recall whether any JNA representatives were at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I remember seeing Vukasinovic and Sljivancanin there. This was in a -- in the informal discussion before the meeting started. I don't know if they were there during the meeting. But they were there during this informal bit before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall any other JNA officers who were -- perhaps you didn't see them at the meeting itself but in the -- in the environs of the --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I also saw Panic at Velepromet. But I don't know if he was there for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us who this Panic was.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He was deputy to Commander Mrksic, deputy for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall his first name or at least his -- his rank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Milorad Panic perhaps? I'm not sure about his first name. As for his rank, major or lieutenant-colonel. I'm not sure about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I may just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just noticed the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Jaksic, we take our second break now, 30 minutes as well. And we'll come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, before the break, you mentioned that after the second time you went to the Velepromet, from there, you went to Petrova Gora. Can you tell us, why did you go to Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I went to report that Mr. Hadzic was coming. I also went because of Milka Keric's son who had gone missing. She asked me it find him. That is the lady who broke through the line to report on two guards' vehicles that had been captured and wanted to find out where the soldiers were. I passed by the barracks on the way and I saw Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll get to that trip to the barracks in a moment. But before we do, did Mr. Hadzic tell you why he wanted to go to Petrova Gora that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He wasn't at Petrova Gora during the entire war-time-period. He wanted to see what the situation was like there after the war, and he wanted to see what had been destroyed. He quite simply wanted to pay a visit to the inhabitants, the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned on your way to Petrova Gora, you stopped at the barracks and you had -- you encountered Mr. Vujovic and Mr. Vojanovic. Yes, Vojanovic is the second name. These are your former commanders of the TO companies - is that correct? - your former TO commanders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd company, yes of the 1st and 2nd company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you encountered them, did you have a conversation with them; and, if so, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The barracks is 100 or 300 metres from Velepromet, and when I saw this on the GPS, I stopped. I saw buses with civilians I told them that I had seen Mr. Mrksic, that I was looking for Vojnovic and the civilians were all going to Serbia. And I just continued to Petrova Gora then. I didn't really linger on there with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How did they react to what you told them with regard to Mr. Mrksic's, or Colonel Mrksic's decision?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They were also angry why weren't they to be left there and be put on trial there, why did they have to go to Serbia ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, I can see from the interpreters booth, you really do need to slow down in your answers, because we're not catching everything that you're saying. Can you please tell us again about how did they react to what you told them about Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They were revolted. They were angry. Why wouldn't they remain there to be put on trial? Why did they have to go to Serbia? So they felt revolted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you regarding why they believed they should stay in the area to be tried?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: All I remember is that this is what I conveyed to them, and then I continued to Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to wait for the question to be completed before answering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, you have to wait for Mr. Olmsted finishing his question before you start answering. Even -- even if you want to add something to your previous answer while Mr. Olmsted is speaking, you should wait. Because, if not, it gets a complete mess for the interpreters. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it appears that maybe you understand a bit of English, and if that's the case, look at the screen in front of you, and when the typing stops, then you know that you can go ahead and answer my question. Because you seem to be predicting my question. Let me just ask my last question one last time. Did Vujovic and Vujnovic tell you why they believed that these prisoners, war criminals should be tried in the SBWS? Did they give you their views?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, they were of the same opinion as Mr. Vujnovic. They believed they shouldn't go to Serbia, since crimes had been perpetrated in that area that is where they should be put on trial. And, finally, it turned out that those who were convicted in Serbia for crimes ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... who had a lot of blood on their hands, these individuals were allowed to go to Croatia, and they didn't serve their sentence. No punishment was meted out to them. Mr. Panic let them go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mention Mr. Panic. Who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Milan Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. I think he was the prime minister at the time of Milosevic. He came over from America.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for clarifying that for me. Other than your conversation with Mr. Hadzic regarding visiting Petrova Gora that day, did you speak with Goran Hadzic about any other issues?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We only said that it would be good if I could exert some influence so that the civilian authorities took over from the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's try to clarify it, "We only said." Who said this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what influence did he want you to use?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, since I was at Petrova Gora and I knew quite a few people there whom I could consult and to whom I could make suggestions, it probably had to do with that. He suggested that the president of the Executive Council of the municipality, Mr. Rajko Bubic [as interpreted] should be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The transcript says "Rajko Bubic." Is that the correct last name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Bibic. Bibic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have L57 on the screen. Yes, I'm sorry, Exhibit L57.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, this is -- this is an Official Gazette for the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I want to turn to page 26 of the original; page 73 going onto page 74 of the English translation. And I'd like to draw your attention to the decision that's beginning on the bottom left side. And we see that this ... hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm actually -- for the original version, I'm looking for the one that has the stamp of 02809343. I'm now informed that that's actually page 16. So I was off by ten. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can look at the bottom left side, bottom decision, we see that this is a 3 December 1991 decision that appoints Srbobran Bibic of Negoslavci chairman of the Executive Council of Vukovar municipality. Sir, can you tell us is this same person as Rajko Bibic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps as a typo. I believe that his name is Rajko. That's the name I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What role did you play in his getting appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember having been involved at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, returning to the timeline of events, you -- you've spoken about stopping by the barracks and you've also spoken about going to Petrova Gora to announce that Mr. Hadzic would soon be there. After you did this, did you return to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from there, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Then Goran Hadzic and Slavko Dokmanovic set off with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who else do you recall came along with you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I first drove off in my vehicle. I was followed by Mr. Hadzic. And Mr. Hadzic was followed by Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone else who came along with you that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic have a security detail?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. At the time, we just drove down in the car, the two of us were together. As for whether there was security detail with us or behind us, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you end up in Petrova Gora that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic and I did. After we had passed by the barracks and reached the medical clinic, the medical clinic you turn left to Petrova Gora. There is a big park there, and they opened fire there from automatic rifles. It was like a battle-field. I noticed in the rear-view mirror that Mr. Dokmanovic was in a sort of a canal, a small canal. He managed to get out of there. We turned off to Petrova Gora. When we arrived there, Mr. Dokmanovic wasn't behind us. He had stayed behind. He returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did you and Mr. Hadzic do in Petrova Gora that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was a euphoria because of the liberation. People were on the street. They were greeting each other, and they would speak to each other informally. There weren't any meeting of any kind. We just passed through and as we passed through, we would greet the people, the inhabitants, we would speak to them, but there was nothing of an official nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how were the people reacting to Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They were delighted. They approached him from all sides. They congratulated him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall Mr. Hadzic telling the people anything during this visit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him having said anything of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And roughly how long were you in Petrova Gora with Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We walked down the entire street and stopped over here and there. So by the time we had done that, it was already the afternoon, perhaps 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly how long you were in Petrova Gora for? Was it an hour? Two hours? Three hours?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Petrova Gora, the street there isn't a very long one, so it didn't take us that long to go down that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you can't really recall how long you were in Petrova Gora at that -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It wasn't for very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah. And where did you go from there? What happened after this visit to Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As my house was in the vicinity, I returned home, and Mr. Hadzic went his own way. We took leave of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Hadzic went that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At the time, it wasn't possible to pass through Vukovar by car. You had to go to Serbia via Sid. For the northern part, if you wanted to go to Serbia, it was only possible to do so if you travelled via Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did Mr. Hadzic go to Sid that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He certainly did. I saw footage. There was nowhere else to go. You couldn't go down through the town. You had to pass through Sid. Whether you wanted to go to Erdut or to Serbia, it was necessary to pass through Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And given the conditions that existed at the time, how long would it take to get from Vukovar town to Sid?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour. Because the -- the road had been damaged by tanks, so you had to drive slowly there. So perhaps it would take about an hour because the roads had sustained significant damage because of the tanks that used them. This road is the road at Oriolik, the road that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, at this time of the year, towards the end of November, what time did the sun set? What time does the sun set? I'm sure it's quite similar today as it was 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I would say around 6.00, half past 6.00, something like that. Half past 5.00, 6.00, 7.00. I don't know, but the days are quite -- a lot shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, after the 20th of November, did you learn about what happened at Ovcara on the night of the 20th and 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were rumours, but a lot later. I think that at the time an investigation had already been launched and there was a lot of media coverage of the event. People had started discussing the matter, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't possible to believe everything that you heard via the media. Because, after the war, many who hadn't participated in combat attributed many things to themselves. So there was no concrete evidence. I wasn't certain about this event. I didn't believe that it had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you eventually learn who the physical perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was at the trial of the Ovcara group in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who were the accused in that case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic was one of the accused, as well as Stanko Vujanovic, Stanko's wife. Vujo Zlatar was also accused. He was acquitted. He was wounded. He hadn't been there. There was Vojnovic, Milan Vojnovic, I think, his name was. I can't remember the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, had you remained TO commander in Vukovar, would you have allowed the massacre in Ovcara to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Serbian soldiers never wanted to commit acts of genocide or to kill helpless civilians. They would have provided security to ensure that tasks could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you were about to answer -- or -- were in the process of answering my question, which is: What actions as TO commander would you have taken to protect those victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: If I had responsibility for prisoners, then I would designate reliable people to deal with the issue. I'd have people who would guarantee with their lives that nothing would happen to these people until the trial started, until they were delivered to a court or a prison, but for as long as they were my responsibility, it is quite certain that no harm would have come to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar, did you remain in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I remained in town until the time of the integration, and after the integration, up until the 22nd of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in 1991, did you establish any business in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What did you do after you left the TO? Did you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Established a transport company. It was the former Cazmatrans. There were four vehicles. We repaired the other vehicles that had been damaged in the war, and there was a donation of about 32 vehicles, and I used these resources to establish a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did you live in Vukovar after the -- after its fall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I lived in my house in Vukovar in Solidarnost Street. Petrova Gora Street and Solidarnost Street intersect. So I lived in my home there, in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did your family return to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the liberation I returned them there. My wife and children returned from Kragujevac, in fact. My elderly daughter was shocked when she saw Vukovar. She spent one night there, no more, and then she returned back, my son as well. The small children and my wife, however, remained in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Zivanovic, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although we got acquainted the day before yesterday, I will introduce myself formally for the record. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzic in this case. You said today that at the time when this crisis broke out in Croatia, your family, that's to say, your wife and four children, left for Kragujevac. Can you explain to us a bit further what the reasons were for your separation, why you stayed behind in Vukovar, while your family left for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was no room for the Serbs at the workplace in Vukovar. I barely managed to get out after my annual leave. After the 2nd of May, I took up annual leave to see what the situation would be like, whether the army would be taking any steps, and how things would unfold. As I ran out of annual leave, I went back to work. All my work-mates - who were Croats, naturally because all the Serbs had left by then - were surprised to see me show up for work. It was before the end of working hours at 12.00 a.m. that we set off. There was a blockade on. There were strict checks in force. Close to the forest of Djergaj on the edge, there was one of their check-points there, a barricade. I was driven by a colleague of mine, Croat, and another one, we were friends. We went together. We were stopped by a policeman at the check-point. He was an experienced policeman who had been there in the previous Yugoslav police structure. He asked for our IDs, took our documents, and he motioned to a group of ZNGs who were close by, beckoning him to take over. Since the colleague who was driving us, Zarko Kordic, appeared to be a Serb, in fact, judging by his name, he believed him to be a Serb, most probably, so started harassing him, provoking him. Later on, I found out that he was in their big structures there. He opposed him, and then he asked him, Did you brush your teeth? The other one said, What? This was to mean that he bad breath because he was a Serb. However, those people from the police told him that he wasn't a Serb, in fact, that I was the only one who was a Serb there. So he gave us back our IDs so that we may pass through. By the time a Hungarian had been killed at Luzac, Jovan Jakovljevic, aka Rakice [phoen], had been killed as well, I believe. Zeljko Pajic had disappeared and it was no longer safe for me to go to work. Every night, fire would be opened at Serb houses. Serb stores or work-shops would be blown up. The news-stand near the barracks had been blown up twice. The most recent occasion provoked objections on the parts of the Croats because the explosion tore the overhead cables, electricity cables, prompting a power outage. And all this simply to make it impossible for the military personnel to buy newspapers. Next, check-points were erected on the edge of Vukovar, later to be followed by others in the centre of town and in all the streets. We came up to be blocked as if we were in a ghetto. And the same went for the barracks as well. Cars were being blown up. That day, when I went to work, at the gate outside the Cazmatrans company, several metres away from the Djergaj forest and the military storage facility there, there was a check-point that they had behind the compound of the company. They were obstacles made out of railway tracks. They were to hinder passage. There were concrete-made pyramids placed on the roadway. They placed anti-tank mines. They were electronically connected. Actually, they were connected by wires so that they could all be activated at once. The passing vehicles could not accelerate further than 5 or 10 kilometres per hour because they had to zigzag to avoid the obstacles. And it was only passenger vehicles, freight vehicles, because trucks could not even pass through. As soon as the multi-party elections started, and when it became obvious that there was some lawlessness and that the Croatian police were -- admitted the worst possible kind of people from the underworld, ex-convicts, criminals. Rather than protect the law, they were precisely the ones who opened fire on -- on Serb homes and blew up their shops. Serbs were getting killed, went missing. Their homes came under fire. And, because of all of this, we were compelled to organise shifts of duty or village guards to protect ourselves so that they would not raid our neighbourhoods and do evil. Since obstacles and barricades were placed everywhere along the street, not just at ends of streets but midway as well, everything was under a blockade. My wife, as she was leaving with the children, at that point, the Croats were already storming into homes, looking for Serb men. None were allowed to leave, and if anyone stayed within, their lives were at risk. From previous experience of their method of attack and the way they proceeded I organised the remaining population in that small nucleus of the neighbourhood. I organised them into squads and platoons, based on my military knowledge. We used the weapons that we had. Some individuals bought homemade weapons, and it was on this basis that we formed the Petrova Gora detachment. Since both we and the barracks there were completely blocked, we were without electricity, water, or telephone lines, it meant that we weren't able to follow what was going on either on TV, on the media in general. We weren't able to communicate. This situation continued for some 20 days. In view of the situation, I decided that we should break our way through to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you've already discussed this. We will possibly go back to that later. My question was what the reasons were for your family's departure to Serbia and your stay in Vukovar. But I think your answer to that question was quite a detailed one. If I may ask you this: Can you describe this in further detail? All the events that you've just discussed now, did they happen after the HDZ came to power, before they came to power, or was it during the election campaign?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was an indication of this cooling of mutual relations during the election campaign. And then, as the HDZ came to power, it escalated fully. There was general lawlessness, mistreatment at the workplace, in the street. People disappearing. The police failing to react to that. And we were their people, after all. Had they tried to take steps politically, they could have asked for negotiations and for a way out of this so that we may live there as free citizens. Instead, they exerted pressure, torture, liquidations. We were left with no other choice than to get organised and defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the multi-party elections, were you aware of the sort of policies that the HDZ advocated? Was it common knowledge among the people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was knowledge of it because it had been publicly announced that the Serbs would be divested of all of their rights. The Serbs were in a constituent nation in the Republic of Croatia. As the HDZ came to power, they lost that right. Not to speak of what had been going on, in towns, at the work-place, they managed to split families apart. There were quite a few mixed marriages. It all suffered as the HDZ came to power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the HDZ policy with regard to Yugoslavia itself or Croatia becoming independent known at all? Did they discuss this publicly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the first policy that became quite known while Yugoslavia was still in existence was the footage involving Spegelj where it was said that grenades were held into Serb homes, that executions were under way. This is something that the Serbs had felt in World War II. Perhaps as many as a million Serbs were killed in Croatia alone during World War II. In my village, some hundred Serbs were killed out of 120 victims of the Fascist terror. The people were loyal. There was no resistance, but they would come, kill people, and had it not been for the dugouts, nobody would have come out of it alive. And I'm talking about World War II. In 1971, with the emergence of the Croatian nationalism of the Maspok, this was a repeat of what had happened later -- what happened later in 1991. There were people who we were on visiting terms with and they would turn their backs to us at one point. Then they started drawing up lists of Serbs who were to be executed. And back then, in 1971, there were many villages where the Serbs organised themselves into village guards in order to protect themselves. In 1991, all of this practically escalated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should be more precise with my questions. At the time, during the election campaign, did the HDZ present its platform with regard to Croatia coming out of Yugoslavia? Was it part of their policy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was something that they talked about in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke today about the organisation of the Territorial Defence as it existed in the pre-crisis period in the former Yugoslavia, and you then explained to us how it all developed. If my understanding of your words is correct, as the political crisis began, as well as the hostilities themselves, the pre-war TO continued to exist or it only continued to exist on paper because it had been of mixed composition and it was no longer a multi-ethnic organisation in the true sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In the early days of the Yugoslav crisis, the TO changed in Slovenia, because the TO Slovenia attacked the JNA barracks. So already at that point, quite a lot of blood was shed. The Slovenians were able to do this because they were ethnically pure and had Slovenians in their ranks. There was a handful of Serbs, and they were able to use these units regardless. Croatia was a multi-ethnic area. There were quite a few Serb. In Vukovar, there were even more Serbs than Croats, and, of course, all the other ethnic groups. Most of the officer corps were Serbs. For that reason, they were unable to use that brigade. When Mercep came to power, he took over the TO Staff and the Secretariat for National Defence. So all the records, all the archives were in the municipality, and the archives from the brigades, all these documents fell into his hands. We could no longer form units on the basis of the existing records. We had to organise ourselves independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, we have information here concerning an armed group, its troops were reviewed in the village of Bogdanovici. What I'm interested in is whether you know anything about this, about the arming, in fact, of these troops.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Mercep said for the media, We are forming unarmed detachments. And then he cynically smiled and said that if necessary they will be armed. It was just a matter of propaganda at the stadium when they said unarmed units, but in fact it concerned the ZNG armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned village guards that had been organised at the time. Tell me, were these village guards subsequently called the Territorial Defence when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were the local guards and we formed platoons, squads, and then they became the TO in accordance with the military principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When explaining how the TO was structured and organised, you said that you were appointed as commander of the TO of OG South.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But, at the time Colonel Mrksic didn't authorise this. He said that this was a political post and that this is something that should be discussed after the war. My question, in fact, is as follows: Could you say how it happened that you were appointed as a commander of the TO of OG South?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know that the meeting was being held. There were over 20 villages in OG South, and the commanders from these villages had a meeting in the village of Oriolik. I was appointed as commander of the staff of the TO OG South there without me being aware of the fact. It was only when I was at the line that they informed me of the fact that I had been appointed as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned these villages, this concerns the villages south of the Vuka river?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the south, as far as Mirkovci and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic perhaps think that because of the way the elections were held or -- that it was a political function or what other reasons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He thought if I left my command post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My objection was he asked what Mrksic thought about something, and I thought that would call for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know the reasons for which Mrksic believed the following -- or, rather, were you ever informed why he believed that appointing you would be a political decision and does this have anything to do with the manner in which people were elected that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the TO Staff -- I apologise. The TO Staff would appoint a commander of the staff. Civilian organs would in fact elect them. There was a subordination from the municipality to the districts to the republic or, rather, this was the hierarchy. They weren't under military administration. But in the case of large units such as brigades, in the case of districts, for example, active-duty officers would be brought in who were capable of being in charge. In battalions, you would have reserve forces. From battalion commanders they were all reserve officers, and the men were also reserve men. So the army had no influence. They were under the ministry in terms of the hierarchy, but the ministry is a political body. And since the municipalities didn't have enough resources and significant resources were required, they couldn't establish warehouses for ammunition and so on, so they had military warehouses in which equipment and weapons were kept. The municipal -- municipalities financed clothing, training, and so on and so forth. And depending on the resources the municipality had, the municipality would have a larger unit, better equipped unit. If it had fewer resources, then the units would not be as large and they wouldn't be as well equipped or well armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I read this in a previous testimony. I won't quote it. Perhaps you can remember it yourself. Before the war-time conflict broke out, were the reservist members of the TO issued with military equipment that they perhaps kept at home and then used when they were requested to participate in reviews or training?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All members of TO units would be issued with uniforms with transport bags, combat rations, and they had all this equipment at home. In the case of mobilisation, they would appear in uniform and only weapons would be brought in on such occasions and the unit would be prepared, ready. Everybody would turn up, and they would only be issued with weapons and the unit would be ready to go into combat within a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell me what sort of uniforms they had -- I apologise. How did they compare with the uniforms of members of the regular Yugoslav People's Army? What were the similarities or dissimilarities.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The TO had JNA uniforms but they were M70 uniforms made in the 1970s, because at the time they and we had similar uniforms. Some officers had similar uniforms, similar insignia to those of active-duty uniforms. But later the army had new uniforms, and if there was a surplus of M70 uniforms they would be given to the TO. So the entire TO had M70 uniforms and these are the uniforms that you can see in the footage. I had such a uniform, a uniform that was used by the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did these uniforms differ in any way from the uniforms that reservists had; for example, those from the uniforms that people who were reserve members of the JNA had?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The reserve men in the JNA had the same uniforms as the JNA. When they would be mobilised, the unit, the battalion, would provide them with the same uniforms that they had so they all had the same uniforms. It wasn't possible to have one company with M70 uniforms and another company with camouflage uniforms. So they had the same uniforms. When the new uniforms were introduced what remained, what -- the uniforms that remained were sort of uniforms used for work-related purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So were there similarities? In other words, when you saw a reservist in uniform, let's say in October or November in Vukovar, and when you saw a member of the TO, were their uniforms similar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did they differ? Please explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They didn't have similar uniforms, but the volunteer who reported towards the end who were issued with equipment with the army they didn't have these uniforms. In fact some of them also received camouflage uniforms because they didn't have the other uniforms towards the end. But the entire TO had the uniforms that dated back to the 1970s. That was the kind of uniform that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, do you want to say that some reservists had camouflage uniforms whereas the TO didn't have any camouflage uniforms at all. Is that the difference?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The difference is that the reservists, if they were part of the JNA, just as in the case of volunteers and the TO, in some cases, some of these men could have camouflage uniforms. In Sid, they would be provided with a military uniform, for example, a camouflage uniform, but there were very few such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, if I have understood this clearly from the footage, the uniforms concerned were those winter uniforms that were used in winter. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the JNA's winter units weren't the same as the TO's ones. They also had camouflage uniforms but winter camouflage uniforms. They had camouflage uniforms with fur. The [indiscernible] also had special uniforms. They were also camouflage uniforms but they had certain straps around the collar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the JNA soldiers had camouflage uniforms and the TO didn't have camouflage uniforms, or are you trying to say something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to say is that infantry units, for example, land units, or armoured units, they had camouflage units. The other units had SMB, olive-drab units, so it was just one colour but they were different. The army did not have the M70 uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The army had camouflage uniforms, the new model of camouflage uniforms. They also had winter uniforms. And after the war we would also receive those uniforms. When the Slavonia Banija Corps was formed these are the uniforms we were issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the army did not have these olive-drab uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't have the M70 models of uniforms, the Guards Brigade didn't have such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms. They didn't have olive-drab uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform is green but it's not the same model. It's an olive-drab uniform but it is not the same model.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to burden you anymore with this issue because it is a matter I am unable to clarify. Please could you tell me the following: As of the time that you were at the head of the TO, as you have said, and up until the time you were relieved on the 16th or 17th of November, who were you subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was subordinated to the commander of OG South, Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was throughout the period during which the OG South was there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the units in the field were subordinated to the commander of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before OG South arrived, whom were you subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Before the arrival of OG South, I was subordinated to Lieutenant-Colonel Jokic, the commander of the TO Mitrovica Brigade. No, not of the TO, of the Mitrovica Brigade, the army's Mitrovica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were subordinated to the commander of OG South, to Colonel Mrksic, you would attend meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings were held in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the command of OG South, in it the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in an extract from your previous testimony I noticed that this would usually take place around 4.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It would be in the afternoon. Tasks would be issued for the following day, and there would be a briefing on what had happened in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell me, did all subordinate officers attend those meetings or were these -- or were the special meetings with the TO without the presence of active-duty officers --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: These were meetings that concerned battalion commanders and further up. So company commanders, commanders of lower-level units did not attend those meetings. Only battalion commanders and commanders of units above the level of a battalion. Naturally chiefs or heads of all the combat arms and services were present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was where assignments were issued and reports made on the assignments issued previously.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were assignments of general nature, such as how to deal with the situation in a battle-field, how to deal with civilians, et cetera, and then there were assignments specific to units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a TO unit commander, I had information that all the JNA senior commanding officers had official notebooks that they were issued with where they would note down precisely the assignments that they received and possibly the assignments that they, in turn, issued to their subordinates. Did you have occasion to see this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I used to have these notebooks at a time when I was chief of the TO brigade. All the chiefs or heads of TO brigades used to have these notebooks before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I am correct, they had these official covers, and they were certified by the superior command or commander issuing them; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what uses was made of these notebooks specifically at the time when you were TO commander or, rather, when you were within the TO? Once you've filled in an entire notebook, would you have handed it over to your commander or what would become of it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't have that notebook. During these preparations that we discussed I had a notepad. It was rather large, so I used another one, a smaller one, where I would note down all the orders given from the operative staff, complete with assignments and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that chiefs within TO brigades would have these notebooks. I'd like to know what the standard procedure was when one such notebook was filled out -- to the full and new ones were issued.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, no, they had notebooks of the sort that they would use when they would attend schooling courses. They could be used as simple notepads. They didn't have to be destroyed. You would keep it with you in your military bag. And until you've completely used it up, you didn't have to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "destroyed," was this done by a superior officer, a commission of sorts, or who?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance when I attended the security course all of these notebooks had to be handed in at the end. In other words, whatever you were taught, all the methods and everything else, it all had to be destroyed so it wouldn't end up in -- in the hands of someone you didn't want to. So you perhaps could keep some of your notes, but not everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But this was specific to security, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- indeed, we are going to stop here for the day. But before I do that, I must remind you for tomorrow that you have to respect a pause between your answer and Mr. Zivanovic's question. Particularly because you speak the same language. Interpreters are still busy interpreting Mr. Zivanovic's question when you already starting to answer, and that's a mess again. Can you try to remember that for tomorrow? So for tomorrow -- for tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We get carried away and then seem to be having a conversation. I -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's why we keep repeating it without much more, Mr. Jaksic. So this is it for today. We'll see you back -- we'll see you back tomorrow in the courtroom at 9.00, which means that you are not released as a witness, that you are not allowed to discuss your testimony with anybody in the meantime, and that you are not allowed to talk to any of the parties. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of July, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
